claim: SARS-CoV-2 has caused over 430 million infections and 5.9 million deaths as of February 2022.
source: The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has caused over 430 million infections and 5.9 million deaths, as of February 2022 (https://coronavirus.jhu.edu/map.html).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to an external data source (Johns Hopkins University COVID-19 map).

claim: Vaccines from Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna use the mRNA of spike protein.
source: Different types of vaccines, for example, those from Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna using the mRNA of spike (S) protein, are currently available, and there are several FDA approved drug candidates under consideration (Li et al., 2021; Venkadapathi et al., 2021; Alvarado et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Li et al., 2021; Venkadapathi et al., 2021; Alvarado et al., 2022).

claim: More infectious mutants such as B.1.617.2 (Delta), B.1.427/B.1.429 (Epsilon), and Omicron have appeared.
source: At the same time, more infectious mutants such as B.1.617.2 (Delta), B.1.427/B.1.429 (Epsilon), and more recently Omicron have appeared (McCallum et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2022), and some evade from the immune system (Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Gobeil et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (McCallum et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2022; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Gobeil et al., 2021).

claim: Some SARS-CoV-2 mutants evade from the immune system.
source: At the same time, more infectious mutants such as B.1.617.2 (Delta), B.1.427/B.1.429 (Epsilon), and more recently Omicron have appeared (McCallum et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2022), and some evade from the immune system (Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Gobeil et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Gobeil et al., 2021).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 can infect a wide range of vertebrates, which could act as a reservoir.
source: Furthermore, the virus's ability to infect a wide range of vertebrates, which could act as a reservoir, points out the future risk despite the vaccination progress (Prince et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to scientific literature (Prince et al., 2021).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped positive single-stranded RNA virus with a genome of approximately 30 kb encoding 29 proteins.
source: SARS-CoV-2, an enveloped positive single-stranded RNA virus, has a large genome of approximately 30 kb encoding 29 proteins (V'kovski et al., 2021; Finkel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (V'kovski et al., 2021; Finkel et al., 2021).

claim: S-protein is a transmembrane homotrimeric class I fusion glycoprotein that plays a critical role in viral cell entry.
source: A transmembrane homotrimeric class I fusion glycoprotein decorating the virus, known as S-protein, plays a critical role in the viral cell entry (Ke et al., 2020; Shang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Ke et al., 2020; Shang et al., 2020).

claim: More than 300 S-protein structures determined with cryo-electron microscopy and X-ray crystallography have been reported.
source: In an immediate response to the pandemic, more than 300 S-protein structures determined with cryo-electron microscopy (EM) and X-ray crystallography have been reported and rapidly advanced in our understanding of the S-protein/receptor binding mechanisms (Wrobel et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020a; Wrapp et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Wrobel et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020a; Wrapp et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020).

claim: The N-terminal subunit (S1) of S-protein is composed of the N-terminal domain (NTD), the receptor binding domain (RBD), and two other subdomains (SD1 and SD2).
source: The N-terminal subunit (S1), which is composed of the N-terminal domain (NTD), the receptor binding domain (RBD), and two other subdomains (SD1 and SD2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Wrapp et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020), initially binds to the host cell receptor angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) (Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Wrapp et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020) and a reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: S1 subunit initially binds to the host cell receptor angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2).
source: The N-terminal subunit (S1), which is composed of the N-terminal domain (NTD), the receptor binding domain (RBD), and two other subdomains (SD1 and SD2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Wrapp et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020), initially binds to the host cell receptor angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) (Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to scientific literature (Yan et al., 2020).

claim: ACE2 binding is followed by priming of the C-terminal subunit (S2) and its large conformational changes leading to membrane fusion for cell entry.
source: This binding is followed by priming of the C-terminal subunit (S2) and its large conformational changes leading to the membrane fusion for the cell entry (Shang et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Shang et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020).

claim: S-protein is covered by 66 N-glycans, 22 per protomer, to evade from the host cell immune system.
source: S-protein is covered by 66 N-glycans, 22 per protomer, to evade from the host cell immune system (Grant et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Grant et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020).

claim: RBDs can take Down or several Up forms including one-Up, two-Up, and three-Up conformations.
source: Numerous cryo-EM structures have revealed that RBDs can take Down or several Up forms including one-Up, two-Up, and three-Up conformations (Figure 1a; Wrobel et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020a; Wrapp et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020b; Juraszek et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Wrobel et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020a; Wrapp et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020b; Juraszek et al., 2021) and a reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Up forms of RBD are accessible to the ACE2 receptor in cell entry, while the Down form is inaccessible.
source: Up forms are accessible to the ACE2 receptor in the cell entry, while the Down is inaccessible (Wrapp et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Wrapp et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021).

claim: Most cryo-EM structures representing Up forms were determined together with other proteins, such as antibodies or a fragment of ACE2.
source: Note that most of the cryo-EM structures representing Up forms were determined together with other proteins, such as antibodies or a fragment of ACE2 (Supplementary file 1A, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to Supplementary file 1A, Table 1.

claim: A single molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) experiment suggested that the RBD Down-to-Up transition occurs even without any ligand of S-protein.
source: A recent single molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) experiment suggested that the RBD Down-to-Up transition occurs even without any ligand of S-protein, and at least one transient intermediate exists during the transition (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to scientific literature (Lu et al., 2020).

claim: At least one transient intermediate exists during the RBD Down-to-Up transition.
source: A recent single molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) experiment suggested that the RBD Down-to-Up transition occurs even without any ligand of S-protein, and at least one transient intermediate exists during the transition (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to scientific literature (Lu et al., 2020).

claim: Several microsecond-scale MD simulations showed the conformational flexibility of the stalk region in S-protein.
source: Several microsecond-scale simulations showed the conformational flexibility of the stalk region in S-protein, different levels of glycan shielding between Down and Up, and their relevance in the ACE2 binding (Grant et al., 2020; Turoňová et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2021; Pavlova et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Grant et al., 2020; Turoňová et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2021; Pavlova et al., 2021).

claim: MD simulations identified specific interactions between side-chain residues or those with glycans to stabilize either Down or Up structure.
source: They also identified specific interactions between side-chain residues or those with glycans to stabilize either Down or Up structure (Casalino et al., 2020; Mori et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Casalino et al., 2020; Mori et al., 2021).

claim: The timescale of the Down-to-Up transition in S-protein is far slower than that attainable in current MD simulations.
source: However, the timescale of the Down-to-Up transition in S-protein is far slower than that is attainable in the current MD simulations, leaving the inherent flexibility and transition pathways largely unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the limitations of current MD simulation timescales.

claim: Enhanced sampling methods including targeted MD, steering MD, nudged elastic band/umbrella sampling, two-dimensional umbrella sampling, adaptive sampling, and weighted ensemble methods have been applied to investigate the RBD transition from Down to one-Up.
source: Therefore, several enhanced sampling methods including targeted MD (Mori et al., 2021), steering MD (Gur et al., 2020), nudged elastic band/umbrella sampling (Simmerling et al., 2020), two-dimensional umbrella sampling (Pang et al., 2021), adaptive sampling (Zimmerman et al., 2021), and weighted ensemble methods have been applied to investigate the RBD transition from Down to one-Up (Sztain et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Mori et al., 2021; Gur et al., 2020; Simmerling et al., 2020; Pang et al., 2021; Zimmerman et al., 2021; Sztain et al., 2021).

claim: In previous enhanced sampling simulations, pre-defined reaction coordinates and/or bias potentials were used to enhance the motions of a single RBD.
source: In these simulations, pre-defined reaction coordinates and/or bias potentials along the coordinates were used to enhance the motions of a single RBD, which limit the number of RBDs to be investigated simultaneously.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the description of previous simulation methods.

claim: gREST_SSCR can enhance domain motions of a protein by exchanging the solute temperature of selected surface residues between neighboring replicas.
source: Here, we apply the generalized replica exchange with solute tempering of selected surface charged residues (gREST_SSCR) (Dokainish and Sugita, 2021), which can enhance domain motions of a protein by exchanging the solute temperature of selected surface residues between neighboring replicas like the original gREST method (Kamiya and Sugita, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature (Dokainish and Sugita, 2021; Kamiya and Sugita, 2018).

claim: gREST_SSCR does not use reaction coordinates or bias potentials.
source: gREST_SSCR is distinct from the other simulations applied to S-protein in that no reaction coordinates as well as bias potentials are used, allowing us to examine the inherent flexibility of S-protein involving more than one RBD.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the gREST_SSCR method.

claim: Down, one-Up, one-Open, and two-Up-like structures were observed in enhanced molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Here, we observe Down, one-Up, one-Open, and two-Up-like structures in enhanced molecular dynamics simulations, and characterize the transition pathways via inter-domain interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: Transient salt-bridges between RBDA and RBDC support RBDA motions from Down to one-Up.
source: Transient salt-bridges between RBDA and RBDC and the interaction with glycan at N343B support RBDA motions from Down to one-Up.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: Interaction with glycan at N343B supports RBDA motions from Down to one-Up.
source: Transient salt-bridges between RBDA and RBDC and the interaction with glycan at N343B support RBDA motions from Down to one-Up.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: Reduced interactions between RBDA and RBDB in one-Up induce RBDB motions toward two-Up.
source: Reduced interactions between RBDA and RBDB in one-Up induce RBDB motions toward two-Up.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: The simulations overall agree with cryo-electron microscopy structure distributions and FRET experiments.
source: The simulations overall agree with cryo-electron microscopy structure distributions and FRET experiments and provide hidden functional structures, namely, intermediates along Down-to-one-Up transition with druggable cryptic pockets as well as one-Open with a maximum exposed RBD.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of simulation data with experimental data (cryo-EM and FRET).

claim: The simulations provide intermediates along Down-to-one-Up transition with druggable cryptic pockets.
source: The simulations overall agree with cryo-electron microscopy structure distributions and FRET experiments and provide hidden functional structures, namely, intermediates along Down-to-one-Up transition with druggable cryptic pockets as well as one-Open with a maximum exposed RBD.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: The simulations provide one-Open structure with a maximum exposed RBD.
source: The simulations overall agree with cryo-electron microscopy structure distributions and FRET experiments and provide hidden functional structures, namely, intermediates along Down-to-one-Up transition with druggable cryptic pockets as well as one-Open with a maximum exposed RBD.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: Eight pairs of positively and negatively charged residues at RBD interface in each chain were selected as solute in gREST_SSCR.
source: Eight pairs of positively and negatively charged residues at RBD interface in each chain were selected as solute in gREST_SSCR and their Coulomb and Lennard-Jones interactions were scaled using solute temperatures in 16 copies of the original systems (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the simulation setup and a reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: MD simulations for longer than 15 µs, in total, were carried out for the solvated S-protein including about 655,000 atoms.
source: MD simulations for longer than 15 µs, in total, were carried out for the solvated S-protein including about 655,000 atoms.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the simulation setup.

claim: RBD motions are drastically enhanced in all three gREST_SSCR simulations.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 4 indicates that RBD motions are drastically enhanced in all three simulations.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Two-Up-like conformations were observed in some replicas of gREST_SSCR simulations.
source: Even two-Up-like conformations were observed in some replicas, for instance, replica 8 in gREST_Down, replica 4 in gREST_Up, and replica 16 in gREST_Down w/o glycan (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Intra-domain structures of three RBDs and NTDs were kept stable during the simulations.
source: Despite the large-scale motions, intra-domain structures of three RBDs and NTDs were kept stable (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: As of September 2021, over 300 cryo-EM structures of S-protein were deposited in Protein Data Bank.
source: As of September 2021, over 300 cryo-EM structures of S-protein, including all Down, one-Up, two-Up, and three-Up conformations, were deposited in Protein Data Bank (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The first principal component (PC1) represents a symmetric Down-to-Up motion involving all three RBDs.
source: In Figure 1b, the first principal component (PC1) represents a symmetric Down-to-Up motion involving all three RBDs, while the second component (PC2) reveals an asymmetric motion of RBDs where only RBDA undergoes the Down-to-Up motion.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The second principal component (PC2) reveals an asymmetric motion of RBDs where only RBDA undergoes the Down-to-Up motion.
source: In Figure 1b, the first principal component (PC1) represents a symmetric Down-to-Up motion involving all three RBDs, while the second component (PC2) reveals an asymmetric motion of RBDs where only RBDA undergoes the Down-to-Up motion.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The two lowest PCs cover about 85% of the conformational variations observed in the cryo-EM structures.
source: The two lowest PCs cover about 85% of the conformational variations observed in the cryo-EM structures.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the principal component analysis.

claim: gREST_Down samples from Down to one-Up conformations.
source: Instead, gREST_SSCR could fill the gap effectively: gREST_Down samples from Down to one-Up, while gREST_Up covers one-Up and two-Up ensembles.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the simulations shown in Figure 1c.

claim: gREST_Up covers one-Up and two-Up ensembles.
source: Instead, gREST_SSCR could fill the gap effectively: gREST_Down samples from Down to one-Up, while gREST_Up covers one-Up and two-Up ensembles.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the simulations shown in Figure 1c.

claim: gREST_Down w/o glycan gives a wider conformational space than gREST_Down.
source: gREST_Down w/o glycan gives a wider conformational space than gREST_Down, suggesting that glycans on the surface of S-protein play key roles in the conformational stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the simulations shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Glycans on the surface of S-protein play key roles in the conformational stability.
source: gREST_Down w/o glycan gives a wider conformational space than gREST_Down, suggesting that glycans on the surface of S-protein play key roles in the conformational stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of simulations with and without glycans.

claim: The gREST_SSCR distributions at 310 K on the hinge-twist angle space well overlap with those of the 891 protomers in the 300 cryo-EM structures.
source: The gREST_SSCR distributions at 310 K on the hinge-twist angle space (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) well overlap with those of the 891 protomers in the 300 cryo-EM structures, as we found on the PC1-PC2 space.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cMD simulation of a single monomer of SD1 and RBD in the Up form sampled Down, one-Up, and one-Open states within 300 ns.
source: Interestingly, the cMD simulation consisting of only a single monomer of SD1 and RBD in the Up form (Monomer_Up in Table 1) sampled Down, one-Up, and one-Open states within 300 ns and gave the structure ensemble close to the cryo-EM structure distributions and the gREST simulations containing a whole S-protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the Monomer_Up simulation.

claim: Four major structures were identified: Down symmetric (DownSym), one-Up (1U), one-Up-open (1UO), and two-Up-like (2UL).
source: Taking together the ensemble distributions on the PC1-PC2 and the HingeA-HingeB spaces, four major structures were identified: Down symmetric (DownSym: (HingeA, HingeB) = (114.9°, 112.5°)), one-Up (1U: (158.3°, 112.7°)), one-Up-open (1UO: (163.3°, 108.9°)), and two-Up-like (2UL: (150.6°, 148.6°)).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the simulations.

claim: DownSym from simulations is well aligned to the high-resolution cryo-EM structure of Down (PDB:6ZGE) with RMSD of 3.7 Å.
source: DownSym and 1U from our simulations are well aligned to the high-resolution cryo-EM structures of Down (PDB:6ZGE; Wrobel et al., 2020 [RMSD: 3.7 Å]) and one-Up (PDB:6XKL (Hsieh et al., 2020) (RMSD: 3.6 Å)), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing simulation structures to cryo-EM structures.

claim: 1U from simulations is well aligned to the cryo-EM structure of one-Up (PDB:6XKL) with RMSD of 3.6 Å.
source: DownSym and 1U from our simulations are well aligned to the high-resolution cryo-EM structures of Down (PDB:6ZGE; Wrobel et al., 2020 [RMSD: 3.7 Å]) and one-Up (PDB:6XKL (Hsieh et al., 2020) (RMSD: 3.6 Å)), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing simulation structures to cryo-EM structures.

claim: RBDA in 1UO is aligned to one of the RBDs in one of the three-Up structures (PDB:7DCC) with RMSD of 5.4 Å.
source: Intriguingly, RBDA in 1UO is aligned to one of the RBDs in one of the three-Up structures (PDB:7DCC; Zhang et al., 2021b [RMSD: 5.4 Å]).
evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing simulation structures to cryo-EM structures.

claim: 2UL from simulations is aligned with one of the two-Up structures (PDB:6X2B) with RMSD of 5.8 Å.
source: Although 2UL from our simulations remains some interactions between RBDA and RBDB, which is completely lost in two-Up cryo-EM structures, 2UL is aligned with those in one of the two-Up structures (PDB:6X2B; Henderson et al., 2020a [RMSD: 5.8 Å]).
evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing simulation structures to cryo-EM structures.

claim: RBM is rarely exposed in DownSym.
source: RBM is rarely exposed in DownSym, where glycans at N165 and N343 largely shield RBM.
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Glycans at N165 and N343 largely shield RBM in DownSym.
source: RBM is rarely exposed in DownSym, where glycans at N165 and N343 largely shield RBM.
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: RBM SASA increases in 1U and 1UO compared to DownSym.
source: In contrast, RBM SASA increases in 1U and 1UO compared to DownSym, wherein 1UO exhibits the utmost increase, suggesting its potential contribution to the receptor and antibody binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: 1UO exhibits the utmost increase in RBM SASA, suggesting its potential contribution to the receptor and antibody binding.
source: In contrast, RBM SASA increases in 1U and 1UO compared to DownSym, wherein 1UO exhibits the utmost increase, suggesting its potential contribution to the receptor and antibody binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3 and inference about binding potential.

claim: The SASA increases only slightly, even decreases locally around residue C480, in 2UL due to the interactions between RBDA and RBDB.
source: The SASA increases only slightly, even decreases locally around residue C480, in 2UL due to the interactions between RBDA and RBDB.
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: One-Up is the primary target of the receptor and antibody binding.
source: This finding suggests that one-Up is the primary target of the receptor and antibody binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the SASA data.

claim: K417 and N501 are accessible only in one-Up conformations.
source: Focusing on mutational residues of concern (K417, L452, E484, and N501 Harvey et al., 2021), K417 and N501 are accessible only in one-Up conformations.
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutations of K417 and N501 could directly affect the binding with the receptor and antibody.
source: The mutations of these residues could directly affect the binding with the receptor and antibody.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the accessibility data.

claim: E484 is accessible in both Down and Up conformations.
source: On the other hand, E484 is accessible in both Down and Up, inferring a widespread effect of E484 mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: E484 mutations have a widespread effect.
source: On the other hand, E484 is accessible in both Down and Up, inferring a widespread effect of E484 mutations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the accessibility data.

claim: L452 is not accessible in any conformations and is expected to rarely affect the binding with either receptor or antibody in wild type.
source: L452 is not accessible in any conformations and hence is expected to rarely affect the binding with either receptor or antibody in wild type (Valdes-Balbin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3 and a citation to scientific literature (Valdes-Balbin et al., 2021).

claim: Epitope regions of Up conformations are generally less shielded by glycans compared to Down.
source: The epitope regions of Up conformations are generally less shielded by glycans compared to Down (at most 99% de-shielded, Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The epitope SASAs of Class I and II antibodies in 1U and 1UO are significantly large.
source: Notably, the epitope SASAs of Class I and II antibodies in 1U and 1UO are significantly large.
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: C105 (Class I) and C002 (Class II) antibodies in cryo-EM structures are well aligned to 1U and 1UO without steric crash.
source: The C105 (Class I) and C002 (Class II) antibodies in cryo-EM structures are well aligned to 1U and 1UO without steric crash (Figure 3c and see Figure 3—figure supplement 4 for detail).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Class I and II antibodies preferentially bind to 1U and 1UO conformations.
source: These results suggest that Class I and II antibodies preferentially bind to these two conformations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the SASA and alignment data.

claim: The epitope SASA values of Class I antibody are small in 2UL due to the interaction between RBDA and RBDB.
source: The corresponding SASA values are small in 2UL due to the interaction between RBDA and RBDB, leading the Class I antibody difficult to align without steric crash.
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In any Up conformations, the epitope SASAs of Class III antibody is comparable to that of Down, while the region is less shielded by glycans.
source: In any Up conformations, the epitope SASAs of Class III antibody is comparable to that of Down, while the region is less shielded by glycans.
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The S309 (Class III) antibody in cryo-EM structures is well aligned to 1U and 2UL.
source: The S309 (Class III) antibody in cryo-EM structures is still well aligned to 1U and 2UL, rationalizing that the Class III antibodies recognize 'glycoepitopes' (Pinto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c and a citation to scientific literature (Pinto et al., 2020).

claim: Class III antibodies recognize 'glycoepitopes'.
source: The S309 (Class III) antibody in cryo-EM structures is still well aligned to 1U and 2UL, rationalizing that the Class III antibodies recognize 'glycoepitopes' (Pinto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to scientific literature (Pinto et al., 2020).

claim: The epitope region of the Class IV antibody is slightly exposed only in 1UO.
source: Note that the epitope region of the Class IV antibody is slightly exposed only in 1UO.
evidence: The claim is supported by SASA data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Further opening of RBD may allow the binding of the Class IV antibody, such as CR3022.
source: Further opening of RBD may allow the binding of the Class IV antibody, such as CR3022, as suggested in the previous computational study (Zimmerman et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the SASA data and supported by a citation to scientific literature (Zimmerman et al., 2021).

claim: The Up structures from MD simulations are reasonably aligned to those of cryo-EM structures with antibodies.
source: Notably, the Up structures from MD simulations are reasonably aligned to those of cryo-EM structures with antibodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The observation supports an idea of conformer selection regime for antibody bindings.
source: This observation supports an idea of conformer selection regime for antibody bindings.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the alignment data.

claim: Lu et al. characterized four structural ensembles including two types of Down (major and minor), at least one intermediate and one-Up conformations using smFRET.
source: Using smFRET, Lu et al. examined the conformational dynamics of S-protein in the presence or absence of its receptor, hACE2 (Lu et al., 2020). They characterized four structural ensembles including two types of Down (major and minor), at least one intermediate and one-Up conformations, suggesting the inherent flexibility of the RBD region regardless of the receptor binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to scientific literature (Lu et al., 2020).

claim: The 13 micro-clusters were identified from gREST_Down.
source: The 13 micro-clusters were identified from gREST_Down (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) including two clusters representing the symmetric Down (Down_sym: D1Sym and D2Sym), two clusters of asymmetric Down with differences in RBDs twist angle distribution (DownAsym: D1Asym and D2Asym), three clusters with a slight increase in the RBD hinge angle around 120°, (Int1: I1a, I1b, and I1c), three clusters with one RBD hinge angle around 130° (Int2: I2a, I2b, and I2c), two clusters with hinge angle around 140° (Int3: I3a and I3b), and one cluster with an Up-like conformation (1UL).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: From gREST_Up, 13 clusters were identified including 10 clusters representing one-Up conformation (1U: 1Ua-1Uj), two clusters with two-Up-like conformations (2UL: 2UaL and 2UbL) and one-Up open cluster (1UO).
source: Similarly, from gREST_Up, the 13 clusters were identified including 10 clusters representing one-Up conformation (1U: 1Ua-1Uj), two clusters with two-Up-like conformations (2UL: 2UaL and 2UbL) and one-Up open cluster (1UO).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the clustering analysis.
